This relative volume of transactions becomes important when you consider that,
according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, the best estimate for the amount of
all global criminal proceeds available for laundering through the financial system in 2009 was
$1.6 trillion.

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) — Suspicious activity reporting requirements?
statutory.answer: Insufficient information to determine whether 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements are triggered on these facts.
statutory.label: neutral
statutory.reasoning: 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) authorizes/mandates suspicious activity reporting by a “financial institution” when it detects a “suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation,” as implemented by Treasury regulations (including thresholds, covered institutions, and what constitutes a reportable suspicious transaction). The fact pattern describes an import-export trading business (SYN_51886bc1) and a list of large ACH/wire transactions, but it does not identify any covered “financial institution” (e.g., a bank, broker-dealer, MSB) that would have the SAR duty under 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g), nor does it provide facts showing the transactions are “suspicious” (e.g., known/credible red flags, apparent structuring, fraud indicators, sanctions nexus, or other facts suggesting a possible violation). Without (1) confirmation that a 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g)-covered financial institution is involved as the reporting party and (2) facts establishing suspicion of a possible legal/regulatory violation under the applicable SAR rules, applicability cannot be determined. Contiguous phrase in answer and reasoning: “31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) suspicious activity reporting requirements.”
